newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan to ask U.S. Congress for U.N. arrears.
newsitem.headline: Annan to ask U.S. Congress for U.N. arrears.

text.p: Kofi Annan, the newly-chosen U.N. secretary-general, said on Monday he would speak to the U.S. Congress if that was what was necessary to get Washington to pay its debts.
"I think it will be necessary and I am prepared to do so," he said in reference to the $1.3 billion arrears owed by the United States which is bankrupting the world organisation.

"I hope that I'll be able to work with the administration and through them to Congress to get the United States to pay its arrears and to pay it dues because without a stable financial base, it is extremely difficult to carry on reform," he told the Newshour With Jim Lehrer in one of his first U.S. television interviews.
Asked why he wanted the post, he replied, "that's a good question. Someone had to do it and it turns out to be my lot."
"And a friend of mine described it as a job from hell."

Annan, 58, the Ghanaian U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping, was chosen by the 15-member Security Council on Friday to succeed Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, of Egypt, whose candidacy for a second five-year term was torpedoed by the United States.
Annan will be formally appointed on Tuesday by the 185-member General Assembly.

The United States said it opposed Boutros-Ghali because he did not move quickly enough in streamlining the organisation. But Annan, who was supported by Washington, said the organisation had to decide what the purpose of reform was.

"Let me say that the reform is important as we have all discussed," he said. "But before we move forward seriously with reform, we and the member states of this organisation have to decide what sort of United Nations we want -- simply put, what should the business be of the United Nations in a tight financial situation."

As the first secretary-general from sub-Saharan Africa, he said his achievement was an honour not just for Ghana but for Africa as a whole and that two of his opponents would be attending Tuesday's General Assembly session: Amara Essy, foreign minister of the Ivory Coast and Hamid Algabid of Nigeria, the secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference.
His other opponent was Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania, a former U.N. envoy for Burundi now based in Washington.

France backed all three, from French-speaking or francophone countries, against Annan, who on Monday held his first meeting since his selection with Boutros-Ghali as well as France's U.N. ambassador Alain Dejammet.

He said all three of his former opponents for the post were "very, very happy for Africa and they congratulate me as Africans, not as anglophones or francophones. And this is a point that I think is important for all those who see Africa only in terms of francophones and anglophones."
Annan is the first secretary-general to have risen through the U.N. ranks, having joined the organisation more than 30 years ago in a variety of jobs in several different cities.
